title: Shelach: another spirit (Numbers 14:24)
hookLine: Caleb "had another spirit with him" and trusted they could go up

lines: ONE VOICE: WE CAN DO THIS.
cards: The meeting's going badly. Someone has laid out every reason the plan will fail, and they're good reasons. Heads are nodding.
The mood in the room is sliding toward no. Then one person, who saw the same numbers, clears their throat and says: actually, I think we can do this. It's not a comfortable moment.
The room turns to look, and not all the looks are friendly. In Numbers thirteen, that person is named Caleb. He says it to a crowd that's about to cry all night.

teach.b: Caleb, from the tribe of Judah, was one of the twelve scouts. He saw the same walls and the same giants.

As the others' report spreads fear, he quiets the people: let's go up at once and take it; we can certainly do it. The ten answer: we can't; they're stronger than us. That night the whole people weeps.
Then Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes in grief and plead: the land is very, very good. Don't rebel. Don't be afraid of its people; God is with us.
The crowd's answer is to reach for stones. Then God speaks about Caleb: "But My servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed Me fully", he will enter the land.
In Hebrew, ruach acheret: another spirit, a different spirit. Not different eyes; he saw what they saw. A different spirit about what he saw.
The Talmud adds a detail from the scouting trip itself. One verse says they went up into the south and he came to Hebron, singular. Who's he?
The rabbis say it was Caleb, alone, going to Hebron to pray at the graves of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, asking to be saved from the scouts' plan.
In that telling, the different spirit came with work and prayer, and a willingness to stand apart from his own group. And it lasts.
In the book of Joshua, Caleb, now eighty-five, says he's as strong as the day he scouted, and asks for Hebron, giants and all.

how: Caleb and Joshua are remembered in Jewish teaching as the two scouts who trusted; the Talmud's account of Caleb praying alone at the patriarchs' graves in Hebron is often told with this portion.

games.why: Caleb speaks against his own group. God says he had another spirit with him, and he alone of his generation, with Joshua, enters the land.

practice: Think of a place where the mood has slid toward no, a family plan, a team project, a friend who's given up on something, and look honestly at the walls and the giants; Caleb did.
Then ask what a different spirit would see in the same facts, and find one true sentence that begins, we can.

wordCard.voice: Shelach. This week: second chances exist, Egypt wasn't free, would all were prophets, short prayers count, go and see, how you see yourself shows, and now Caleb's different spirit.
